opening: Operations on strings of 0s and 1s, and the right thing to count.

steps.prompt: Split 0011101 into maximal groups of equal neighbouring characters (00, 111, 0, 1). How many groups are there?
In 0011101, at how many places do two neighbouring characters differ?
nudges: Between which positions does the character change?
steps.showed: One fewer than the number of groups: every group but the first begins at such a place.

steps.prompt: Take 0011101 and invert the characters in positions 3 to 5 (the three 1s). How many places with differing neighbours does the result have?
nudges: What does the string look like afterwards?
steps.showed: From three such places down to one.

steps.prompt: A substring is inverted (every 0 becomes 1 and every 1 becomes 0). Which places with differing neighbours can change?
options: Only the two at the ends of the substring; places strictly inside it and outside it stay as they are
nudges: Two neighbours both inside the substring: if they differed before, do they differ after?
What about a neighbour pair with one inside and one outside?
steps.showed: Inside, both neighbours flip together and their relation is unchanged. Only the two edges of the substring can gain or lose a change: at most two per move.

steps.prompt: One move inverts any substring. What is the smallest number of moves that turns 0101010 into all 0s?
nudges: How many separate groups of 1s are there?
Can one move remove two groups of 1s?

steps.prompt: And the smallest number of moves to turn 110011011 into all 0s?
steps.showed: Again the number of groups of 1s; their lengths do not matter.

steps.prompt: One move inverts any substring of a string of 0s and 1s. Prove that the smallest number of moves needed to make every character 0 equals the number of maximal groups of 1s.
claims: Put a 0 in front of and behind the string, and count the places where neighbours differ: with g groups of 1s there are exactly 2g such places, since each group has a left edge and a right edge.
A move changes the relation between neighbours only at the two ends of the inverted substring, so it lowers that count by at most 2.
The all-zero string has count 0, so at least g moves are needed.
Inverting one whole group of 1s removes it, so g moves suffice.
nudges: What quantity is 0 exactly when the string is all 0s?
By how much can one move change it?
steps.showed: Count edges between groups, not characters: a move touches at most two edges.

steps.prompt: One move inverts any substring. What is the smallest number of moves that turns 0011010011 into the alternating string 0101010101?
nudges: Mark the positions where the string disagrees with the target. What does a move do to the marks?
steps.showed: Mark each position as agreeing or disagreeing with the target: inverting a substring inverts the marks there. So it is the same problem on the string of marks: count its groups of disagreements.

steps.prompt: How many strings of 0s and 1s of length 10 consist of exactly 4 groups?
nudges: A string is determined by its first character and what else?
Among the 9 places between neighbours, how many must be changes?
steps.showed: Choose the first character (2 ways) and which 3 of the 9 gaps are changes.

steps.prompt: Take 10000011. You may once choose a substring and invert it. Afterwards you pick as long a subsequence as possible in which neighbouring picked characters differ. What is the largest length you can get?
nudges: The longest such subsequence takes one character from each group. So what are you maximising?
By how much can one move raise the number of groups?
steps.showed: The longest alternating subsequence has one character per group. One inversion adds at most two edges, so at most two groups, and it cannot exceed the length of the string.

steps.prompt: Now make it run. Write a program for the task below; it is judged on large inputs, so the idea has to be in the code.
steps.showed: One pass counting the places where a group of 1s begins.

reveal.name: Blocks and boundaries
reveal.statement: An operation on a substring of a binary string usually changes only the boundaries between blocks of equal characters, and at most the two at the ends of the substring. So count blocks and boundaries, not characters.
reveal.remark: Padding the string with a fixed character on both sides makes every block have two boundaries. To reach a target other than all zeros, first XOR with the target.
